items.title: I’m watching Alaska closely
items.author: 1axbu1qhql2swxa1lge2scp6h8nkgbk7gswfr3@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
items.content:
Whoever said everything is bigger in Texas hasn’t been to Alaska. The Last Frontier is bigger than Texas, California and Montana combined.

The largest national park in the country is in Alaska. Its name is one of my favorites: Wrangell–St. Elias.

But Alaska’s size is more than a point of pride. It also makes voting there remarkably hard. The state’s beautiful but isolated landscape creates complications for voters, and dozens of polling places are in towns without road access.

Voting by mail isn’t simple either, as extreme weather can cause days-long delays. In some remote villages, polling places without election workers fail to open at all.

Though the networks still haven’t called Alaska’s Senate race, it is clear that Mary Peltola is poised to win and become the 56th member of the Senate Democratic caucus come January.

Peltola’s likely victory and its close margin prove two truths. First, every vote matters, and the fight to ensure every vote is counted is essential to democracy. Second, Democrats can win anywhere they have the candidates and resources to compete.

Sadly, Alaska’s elections have also been the target of one of Donald Trump’s fiercest attacks, and he is showing no signs of letting up.

Less than two weeks before Election Day, Trump’s Department of Justice sued to block Alaska from certifying Peltola as the winner if she defeated Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan. My firm, Elias Law Group, intervened on behalf of the Peltola campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee to fight back.

We won: two days before the election, a federal judge dismissed the case. The DOJ has appealed but seems in a hurry to further litigate their defeat.

Then the Trump DOJ launched criminal investigations without being able to confirm that any crime had been committed. In the days before the election, the DOJ leaked that I was among its targets.

Trump has targeted me before. He hates me because I fight and win.

After the 2020 election, I helped lead the legal effort that defeated him and his allies more than 60 times. My firm just helped Scott Colom unseat Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith and win Mississippi’s U.S. Senate race. Now we are fighting in Alaska.

I have no doubt that Trump’s hatred of me is only growing. I wear his scorn as a badge of honor.

But even the best legal work won’t protect democracy from Trump’s lies and smears. That requires pro-democracy platforms and outlets that tell the truth without fear or compromise.

Democracy Docket covered the count in Mississippi from start to finish, and now its team is on the ground in Alaska. The team is watching and reporting closely, bringing readers daily updates and insights as the race unfolds.

I created Democracy Docket for exactly this kind of moment. While other outlets offer horse-race coverage and both-sides analysis, Democracy Docket covers free and fair elections every day of the year through an uncompromisingly pro-democracy lens.

We shine a light on the voting rights fights the national spotlight misses. It breaks down court cases months before Election Day and follows stories years before they reach the front pages of legacy media.

After much discussion, Democracy Docket has decided to keep its paywall down, as it has been since Election Day, until the Alaska race is called. This was not an easy decision.

But as Trump and the GOP continue to spread lies about this election, the stakes are too high to keep anything behind a paywall.

Members keep Democracy Docket’s website and podcasts free for everyone and make it possible to keep the paywall down as the fight for Alaska continues. They also get my written analysis: what’s happening in the courts, what each ruling means for the next election, and where the fight is headed before anyone else is talking about it.

If you’ve been reading my analysis since the paywall came down on Election Day, you already know what you’d be missing.

If you can’t upgrade right now, I understand. As always, thank you for being a subscriber and reader. But if you do, I would deeply appreciate it.

All eyes are on Alaska today, but at Democracy Docket, we will keep our eyes trained on the Last Frontier every day.

The battle for free and fair elections does not end when the networks make their call. It lives on as long as we are willing to fight.

I wish I could say that the Trump administration's lack of professionalism has ceased to amaze me, yet this week’s Veterans Day debacle left me speechless…again. In case you missed it, following a Veterans Day ceremony, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who avoided impeachment by the skin of his teeth the day prior, was reprimanded after his entourage laughed and chatted loudly while visiting the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier in Arlington, Virginia. It’s a sacred monument to honor unidentified soldiers who died in the line of duty.

“All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times,” the sentinel yelled. Seeing the Department of Defense’s group looking like rambunctious middle schoolers on a field trip on such hallowed ground is sad, to say the least. But Hegseth’s entire tenure leading the US military has been riddled with controversy. 

Since taking office, he’s tried to purge

women, transgender people, and people of color from the military’s ranks with blatantly discriminatory policies. He used an unprecedented meeting of generals and admirals to “fat-shame” them. His end goal seems to be returning the military to a time when anyone who wasn’t a straight white man was deemed unfit to serve.

“Black service members and Black veterans understand that we are either not welcome or we will exist within a permanent hierarchy in which white men are at the top,” Kyle Bibby, co-founder of the nonprofit Black Veterans Project, told

host Al Letson. “Particularly straight white men.”, Bibby sits down with Letson to explain what life is like for today’s Black troops and how Hegseth has widened the gap of racial inequities in the military. Listen to it today.

items.title: Why is no one talking about this?
items.author: 1axbu94jjhaneq2wl1qmrqxrtbrs0tar9a47fn@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
items.content:
Earlier this week, amid all the excitement in Mississippi and uncertainty in Alaska, a federal judge quietly closed the book on the Department of Justice’s lawsuit against California. The DOJ had sued to force the state to set aside more than 20,000 ballots it did not want counted.

After aggressively litigating the case all the way to the Supreme Court, and losing at every level, the DOJ asked the court to dismiss its own lawsuit. The court obliged.

Only two weeks ago, the specter of the DOJ prosecuting election officials for counting ballots hung over the Golden State and elections nationwide. We watched as the Trump administration escalated its lies and demands. We worried that this case might be a prelude to seizing ballots.

The order closing the case was a simple one page. But in it, U.S. District Judge David O. Carter offered one last statement explaining what had been at stake:

“This lawsuit attempted to disrupt an ongoing election and create confusion and uncertainty for voters and election workers alike. The right to vote is sacred. So, too, is trust in our democracy.”

These words echo what conservative Third Circuit Judge Stephanos Bibas wrote six years ago when he sternly rejected the Trump campaign’s challenge to the 2020 presidential election in Pennsylvania:

“Free, fair elections are the lifeblood of our democracy. Charges of unfairness are serious. But calling an election unfair does not make it so. Charges require specific allegations and then proof. We have neither here.”

The parallels between November 2020 and today are striking. In both instances, Trump’s party lost hotly contested elections. Both involved litigation Trump instigated to try to change the outcome. And both then and now, the courts soundly rejected his outrageous claims.

Beneath those similarities, however, lie disturbing differences.

The Pennsylvania case in 2020 was litigated by a bumbling Rudy Giuliani on behalf of the Trump campaign. It was the dying gasp of a losing campaign.

The California case, by contrast, was filed by the Department of Justice. It was not born of desperation; it was part of a larger, premeditated attack on free and fair elections.

And while the Pennsylvania lawsuit sought to throw out lawful votes, the California case went further. It was paired with threats to investigate and prosecute state and local election officials.

Perhaps most importantly, the dismissal of the Pennsylvania case was celebrated in the national media as a triumph of democracy over efforts to discredit free and fair elections. The dismissal of the California case this week barely registered outside a handful of outlets.

Over the last two years, there have been many instances of Trump’s aberrant and destructive behavior. None has done more damage to the nation’s identity than his ceaseless attacks on our elections.

But worse than Trump’s conduct is the way it has been normalized in places that once would have found it outrageous and worthy of unsparing condemnation.

If a federal judge can remain judicious while saying the DOJ’s lawsuit “attempted to disrupt an ongoing election,” why can’t the legacy media use similarly direct language? If a court is willing to say the DOJ’s intent was to “create confusion and uncertainty for voters and election workers,” why can’t our civic leaders say the same?

After the 2020 election, for a brief time at least, this was not a problem. After Jan. 6, 2021, the condemnation of Trump was forceful and uncompromising.

He was impeached, and a bipartisan majority of the Senate voted to convict him. Media outlets across the spectrum spoke in clear moral terms. Business leaders pledged to support democracy.

Yet today, as Democrats celebrate their victories and the GOP nurses its wounds, there is near silence about Trump’s assault on voting and elections. It is as if it were a passing phase, a remnant of the pre-election period that we can now forget.

This was the mistake many made after Trump left office the first time. We thought he was gone and his movement discredited. The initial shock and outrage over his behavior wore off. Corporate pledges quietly lapsed. Polite society moved on.

How many more elections must we endure in which the threats reach critical levels? How many more times can we ask lawyers and the courts to bail us out?

In the coming weeks, Democrats will take power in Congress and in states around the country. They must address the threats we have endured for nearly a decade under Trump and the MAGA Republicans.

That means enacting strong new voting laws, protecting voters and election officials from intimidation, and conducting oversight over the executive branch’s unlawful actions.

We as citizens must do our part as well.

That means calling and writing our representatives and demanding that they use every tool available to them. It means showing up when our legislatures debate election laws. And it means standing up, speaking out and working to defeat Trumpism as an ideology.

I understand that there are many other important issues facing our country, from the cost of living to health care. But unless we fix our democracy, none of those other problems will be solved.

Over the next few months, I plan to make this a central theme of my writing and advocacy. I hope you will join me. Subscribe to Democracy Docket to follow along.

It’s been an incredible and hectic week witnessing democracy in action. This election was not just for Mississippi, but an opportunity to put an overlooked state back on the national agenda. People were thrilled to see so much national attention and hope Democratic senator-elect isn’t the end for progress.

The more I spoke to Mississippians, the clearer it became how many roadblocks, by design, there are to voting in the state. I have never witnessed a state that so clearly disenfranchises voters every chance it gets. The Experian data issue helped shed light on a very broken voting system. Voters can only register to vote in person or by mail — not online. Mississippi is one of three states that doesn’t have early voting, and one of 13 that requires an excuse to vote by mail.

And if you vote in the right county but the wrong precinct, your vote will not count. If a poll worker forgets to sign your affidavit ballot, your vote will not count. I could go on, but the point is this was an election won despite all odds stacked against Colom. And having talked to the organizers on the ground, it was truly a grassroots effort to get such a high turnout to the polls.

A lot, a lot, A LOT, of work happened behind the scenes to make history. I hope this conversation regarding Mississippi’s voting practices continues, and ultimately leads to more change. Luckily, Colom already has a , he told us in an exclusive interview.

items.title: Scott Colom prevailed
items.author: delivery_20261112061301.48379211.277@bounce.slate.com
items.content:
The blue tsunami hit over a week ago, and it’s still making waves for Democrats. We’re looking at you Mississippi—one of the reddest states in the country was finally called for Democrat Scott Colom. He will be the first elected Black senator for the state in over 150 years, unseating Republican incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. Colom’s win came down to just a few thousand votes, and each side had lawyered up in anticipation of an ugly legal battle. The entire process has highlighted just how archaic Mississippi’s voting system is, even as—this time—democracy seems to have prevailed.

On Wednesday evening, Mississippi’s senate race was called for Colom, who ended up carrying the state by about 4,600 votes over Hyde-Smith. Now, election officials will finalize remaining affidavit ballots, including ones for voters who had their registrations incorrectly marked inactive after a massive purge of Mississippi’s voter rolls ahead of this year’s midterm elections. Come Friday, county election commissioners for all of Mississippi’s 82 counties have to submit their certified election results to the secretary of state’s office. Then, on December 3, Secretary of State Michael Watson is scheduled to declare the statewide general election results.

The Colom and Hyde-Smith campaigns have indicated they are preparing for potential legal action, with both sides deploying small armies of attorneys and observers to monitor the ballot counting process. Challenging whether certain ballots should be counted is one of the only ways candidates can contest the outcome of a federal Senate race in Mississippi, as it is the only state in the country that does not have a law in place for automatic vote recounts in close races. The state also does not have a law in place mandating runoff elections. That means that Colom and Hyde-Smith must wait until final results of their election are announced before they can file a lawsuit (with the potential to result in a recount), which could happen any time after Friday’s deadline. 

Two days after Election Day, Hyde-Smith’s campaign sent a letter to each county election commissioner and circuit clerk for all 82 Mississippi counties demanding they separate all affidavit ballots from regular and absentee ballots. Affidavit ballots are generally used when a voter does not have their ID or was previously marked as inactive, as was the case for upward of 200,000 Mississippi voters after Watson partnered with credit agency Experian to purge the state’s voter rolls. In order to validate an affidavit ballot, voters have to physically go to their circuit clerk’s office and present their ID within five business days of filing that affidavit ballot in order for it to be counted.

This is a move straight out of the Trump administration’s playbook, as the Justice Department in October similarly demanded California election officials separate mail ballots for about 20,000 voters it claimed it suspected were noncitizens trying to vote. A federal judge ruled against the DOJ, writing that separating ballots would “risk disenfranchising an untold number of voters” and “would wreak havoc and disrupt the election that is already underway” and  “create a chilling effect on election workers and voters alike.”

Nevertheless, Hyde-Smith’s team insisted that separating affidavit ballots is required by Mississippi law and federal law, so that each one “can be verified.” That very same day, Colom’s campaign fired off their own letter to Mississippi’s election officials acknowledging Hyde-Smith’s demands and warning that if they depart from ordinary election procedures, they “will violate Mississippi voters’ rights and Mississippi election law.” So, who’s right here?

Well, the Mississippi Supreme Court ruled on this issue back in 1975 in Clark v. Rankin County Democratic Executive Com.and concluded that separating certain ballots is unlawful because it undermines “the secrecy of a voter’s ballot.” Colom’s campaign also noted that the U.S. Supreme Court’s decision in asserted that the “arbitrary and disparate treatment of voters in its different counties” amounts to “a constitutional violation” of the equal protection clause of the 14th Amendment. 

It’s also worth noting that in the event that Hyde-Smith or Colom is successful in forcing a recount through filing a lawsuit, these types of procedures “ change the results of elections,” as Derek Muller, Notre Dame law professor, noted on the Election Law Blog. So far, the slow dribble of counting affidavit and mail ballots has favored Colom, something he predicted at the outset of Election Day. “The affidavit [ballots] always move in the Democrats favor in Mississippi. If you look at the ballots that are left, it’s going in our favor,” Colom told reporters. 

Mississippi was not on Democrats’ wish list heading into the midterm elections, relegated as a state that was impossible to flip from Republicans, something Colom argued hurts many Southern Democrats. But as his campaign catapulted to the national stage on Election Day and has since captivated the national news media, Mississippi’s Senate race also sheds light on how the state has gotten away with suppressing voting rights for decades. It's one of three states that does not offer early voting, while it requires an excuse to vote by mail. The state also strips individuals convicted of certain felonies of their right to vote. In this race alone, 24 percent of affidavit ballots were rejected for issues such as having an incorrect county registration or the person voting at the incorrect precinct. The rejections appear to have been much more severe in deeply blue counties.

Meanwhile, Mississippi is home to the highest share of Black voters, who account for nearly 40 percent of the state’s population, yet lawmakers have ensured there is only Black-majority district in the entire state. Even that may go away soon, as state Republicans considered redistricting, now a perfectly legal endeavor thanks to the Supreme Court’s decision. However, on Nov. 3, Mississippi voters showed up and showed out in numbers that are proving to be insurmountable, in spite of all the barriers they face.

items.title: The Word of the Day: Accountability
items.author: bounce_a1d1deb5-a5de-f111-91f0-000d3a18e244_prod@bounce.myngp.com
items.content:
Sesame Street once featured a regular segment, , in which Muppet characters and a celebrity guest explained a specific vocabulary word. Their choices evoke nostalgia for words that today are often derided as weakness, for example, diversity, belonging, fairness, and kindness. 

were applied to this post-election climate, two would dominate: Accountability and Affordability. Which should Congress be working to solve? But this is not a binary choice. If that Sesame Street segment existed today, perhaps the wisdom of Big Bird and Elmo could break through the cacophony to explain how interdependent these concepts actually are.

Affordability is built on the rule of law and requires a system of commerce that is fair, predictable, and offers a level playing field for all. If the rules are changed to allow those in power to dole out favors to their friends and supporters while punishing their enemies, affordability for all becomes unachievable.

Accountability provides the foundation for affordability. Just as government leaders are accountable to voters, government lawyers are accountable to the Constitution and to rules of professional conduct, the oath they swore when they became lawyers, and the rules of a fair justice system. If government lawyers are dishonest or mislead the court, fail to adhere to the rules that govern our profession, or attack judges personally for decisions they do not agree with, then the public itself is harmed.

LDAD has helped pioneer the notion that lawyers in the public sphere must be held accountable when they undermine a free and fair election or ignore rules that apply to government agencies and their leaders.This week, LDAD and 53 scholars and retired judges filed an against three senior Department of Justice officials: Harmeet Dhillon, the former Assistant Attorney General for the Civil Rights Division; Robert Keenan, Acting Deputy Assistant Attorney General for the Civil Rights Division; and Eric Neff, Acting Chief of the Voting Section.

The complaint alleges that Ms. Dhillon, Mr. Keenan, and Mr. Neff violated their professional and ethical obligations by pursuing lawsuits against 30 states and the District of Columbia, jurisdictions that refused to provide the Department of Justice with unredacted voter records containing millions of Americans' sensitive personal information, including Social Security numbers, driver's license numbers, addresses, and voting histories, and continued to pursue claims that courts repeatedly rejected as legally unsupported. As of October 23, 2026, DOJ had lost all 27 cases in which courts issued a ruling, as well as the first appellate decision addressing the DOJ’s demands for this voter information. Yet DOJ continued to pursue the same baseless legal theories rejected by the courts.

LDAD also recently sought accountability by filing an against Hugh Evans, a member of the Alabama bar who serves as a special agent of the Federal Bureau of Investigation. The complaint concerns the sworn affidavit Mr. Evans submitted to a U.S. Magistrate Judge in January 2026 to obtain a search warrant for 2020 election records held by Fulton County, Georgia. The FBI executed that warrant on January 28, 2026, seizing more than 650 boxes of ballots and other election materials. The complaint alleges that the affidavit withheld from the court material information: that Georgia election authorities had already investigated and rejected the very allegations on which it relied.

Accountability is a critical . It is the glue that holds the justice system together and the very foundation of the rule of law. It is the pathway to affordability and to all of the rights that we hold dear.

items.title: I spent two years defending these Mississippi ballots
items.author: 1axbxsdl4pgemalky98w4g6g34ie632aghi2eb@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
items.content:
Lawyers like to joke that they went into law to avoid math. But my career has been marked by certain unforgettable numbers.

There is 218, the number of seats a party needs to control the U.S. House. And there’s 60, the number of votes it takes to break a Senate filibuster.

There is 428, Harry Reid’s margin of victory after his 1998 recount. And there’s 312, Al Franken’s margin over Norm Coleman after months of recounts and litigation following the 2008 election.

Today, a new number was burned into my memory: 67. That is how many absentee ballots Hinds County, Mississippi, received, processed and counted in the five business days after Election Day.

To be clear, these voters, like thousands of others across the state, did everything right. They filled out and mailed their absentee ballots by Election Day. Through no fault of their own, slow mail service meant county officials did not receive them until afterward.

In Hinds County, these ballots were reviewed and processed, and as a result, Scott Colom’s lead grew by a net 58 votes.

If Republicans had had their way, these ballots never would have been counted. They would all have been rejected for arriving too late, and the voters who cast them would have been disenfranchised.

I do not make this statement lightly or as a generalization. It is a statement of fact.

In January 2024, the Republican National Committee sued the state of Mississippi to invalidate its law allowing ballots postmarked by Election Day to be counted if they arrive within five business days afterward.

By then, I had already litigated several cases against Republicans over this very issue. Because these ballots tend to skew Democratic, the RNC and its allies have repeatedly fought to have them discarded. Elias Law Group has fought just as hard to have them counted.

The RNC has been candid about its motive. “Late-arriving mail-in ballots that are counted for five additional days,” its lawyers wrote in the Mississippi complaint, “disproportionately break for Democrats.”

In a state where race and party are so closely correlated, they might as well have added that counting ballots cast by Black voters would hurt Republicans’ chances of winning. Hinds County itself is more than 70% Black.

When the RNC sued Mississippi, it seemed clear to me that it was hoping to find a friendly red state that would either quietly settle or, at the very least, not fight back hard. It did not count on my law firm intervening to defend the Mississippi law.

Over the two years that followed, on behalf of Vet Voice Foundation and the Mississippi Alliance for Retired Americans, my firm and I fought the RNC at every level of the federal courts. We won before a conservative federal district judge in Mississippi, only to see that victory reversed by the even more conservative 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals.

Along with the state, we took the case to the U.S. Supreme Court, though few thought we would succeed. But we did.

This past June, the Supreme Court ruled in our favor, 5-4, in Watson v. Republican National Committee.

Writing for the majority, Justice Amy Coney Barrett explained that “by default, responsibility for the mechanics of congressional elections belongs to States.” Those words would come to matter not only in Mississippi but in other cases nationwide.

At the time of the decision, most of the attention focused on what it would mean for the more than a dozen other states with laws similar to Mississippi’s. Few expected it to matter much in a state as Republican as Mississippi itself.

So, when I saw the numbers from Hinds County earlier today and realized what these voters had helped accomplish in the Senate race, I paused. It is not just that these voters would have been disenfranchised for no reason. It is that they would have been denied the chance to be part of history.

Over the last several years, Republicans have relied on the courts to advance their disenfranchisement schemes. The Supreme Court’s 6-3 decision in Louisiana v. Callais, gutting the Voting Rights Act, remains the most prominent example. But hardly the only one.

Republicans thought they would win Watson. As a voting rights lawyer, and as counsel in the case, I was thrilled they did not.

But today, my connection to this case grew deeper. It was no longer just an important precedent. It was a lifeline for democracy and free and fair elections in Mississippi.

Which is why another number will forever be burned into my mind: 4,669. Scott Colom’s margin of victory over Cindy Hyde-Smith to be elected to the U.S. Senate.

items.title: The three names I never forget
items.author: 1axcf6uvpmg4upxuykvh5tibie5q5bh4qw0n9v@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
items.content:
As a child growing up in New York, I knew very little about Mississippi. Other than trips to see my grandparents in Florida and a visit to Arlington National Cemetery, I had never been to the South.

Most of what I knew about Mississippi came from learning about the civil rights era. Even then, to a young boy who had barely traveled outside his own neighborhood, it was mostly a blur of places I had little context to understand.

There was, however, one place and three names I knew well.

Philadelphia, Mississippi, is where three civil rights workers, James Chaney, Andrew Goodman and Michael Schwerner, were abducted and murdered in 1964 by members of the Ku Klux Klan, aided by local law enforcement.

Like me, Goodman and Schwerner were white, Jewish New Yorkers. Chaney was a 21-year-old Black Mississippian from Meridian who had grown up under the very system the three were working to dismantle.

The three men were part of Freedom Summer, the 1964 effort to register Black voters across Mississippi. Growing up, they were held up as examples of the importance of standing up for others' rights, even at great risk and sacrifice.

They also sparked my interest in voting rights and shaped my view of politics.

In 1980, when I was 11, Ronald Reagan campaigned at the Neshoba County Fair, just a few miles from where the three men were killed. Without any mention of them, he told the crowd, “I believe in states’ rights.” Weeks later, he stood in New Jersey and promised to “make America great again.”

Eight years later, when I was in college, the movie “Mississippi Burning” was released. It was loosely based on the events surrounding the murders of Chaney, Goodman and Schwerner.

As I built my legal career, these three men and the cause they championed were never far from my mind. Ahead of the 2020 election, I had the opportunity to work with the Andrew Goodman Foundation on critical litigation to protect young voters.

I will admit that until this year, I did not expect to see a Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from the state where Chaney, Goodman and Schwerner were murdered. Mississippi has not sent a Democrat to the Senate since 1982, and it has not had a Black senator since Reconstruction.

But then again, I had never seen a candidate like Scott Colom.

Colom is an extraordinary public figure: a prosecutor with compassion and an activist who knows how to achieve real change. He is truly a man for this moment.

Last week, when Colom and his campaign needed a law firm to protect his lead, I jumped at the chance, not only because of Mississippi’s past but because of what Colom’s victory would mean for its future.

In the days since, his lead has grown and so has my respect for him.

I am 57 years old now. The stories of the civil rights struggle of the 1960s still linger in my mind. But in addition to being a lawyer, I am now the founder of Democracy Docket, an independent pro-democracy media outlet.

So when the vote counting began in Mississippi, it was clear that Democracy Docket needed to be there to report on and document history in the making.

For the first time, Democracy Docket sent journalists to cover the hour-by-hour, day-by-day developments in a close election. I have also done near-daily livestreams explaining what is happening and why.

While the legacy media has treated this as a horse-race story between a Democrat and a Republican, Democracy Docket has covered it as what it fundamentally is: a story about democracy and free and fair elections.

In the days ahead, I expect Scott Colom to be declared the winner and his election certified. When he takes office in January, I have every reason to believe he will become a critical voice in the fight for voting rights for all.

Donald Trump and his cronies will continue to attack free and fair elections. I will return to the courtroom to stop voter suppression and election subversion.

As I do, I will keep in mind the legacy of James Chaney, Andrew Goodman and Michael Schwerner and what they fought and died for.

That is the spirit I have tried to instill in Democracy Docket. I hope it shows every day.

If you appreciate this work and share Democracy Docket’s commitment to telling the stories that matter most to voters and democracy, please join now. A premium membership gives you access to all of Democracy Docket’s exclusive content. More importantly, it makes possible the kind of coverage this moment demands.

I have come a long way from the young boy growing up in New York learning about Philadelphia, Mississippi, and so has our country. I am proud to be in this fight for Scott Colom and Mississippi voters.

items.title: “60 Minutes” found zero minutes for Trump’s new Big Lie
items.author: 1axboacd0cf9o1fnfu0ms74722xavqooe338gz@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
items.content:
“Does anybody really believe that this ‘Election’ was honest?” Donald Trump posted on Truth Social this morning. “How could the Polls be so wrong??? Some early voting ‘dumps’ were so large that it was impossible to win, no matter how many people went to vote. It’s all about the machines, which are far more important than the voter! President DJT”

With that post, Trump went all in on a new Big Lie, this time about the 2026 midterms. None of this should come as a surprise. I warned about it on my podcast on Sunday.

But you wouldn’t have known it from watching “60 Minutes” that same night.

I spent the better part of an hour on my podcast walking viewers through Trump’s growing embrace of election denialism. The signs were obvious to anyone who bothered to pay attention. Trump had been sharing conspiracy theories and making threats about elections in Alaska. The legacy media ignored them.

I timed the episode to end just before “60 Minutes” began. Trump was being interviewed by Ross Douthat, one of the program’s new conservative correspondents, and I wanted to see whether election denialism would come up.

Douthat asked Trump about UFOs, death and religion. They chatted about forgiveness and about a potential successor to lead the MAGA movement. Yet, he did not ask a single question about Trump’s election denialism.

The only reference to Trump’s attacks on elections came in the segment’s introduction, and, ironically, it falsely credited Trump with having set election denialism aside:

“In the past, this president has met defeat with claims of fraud and the effort to overturn the 2020 election. But when we met with him in the White House on Friday for his first sit-down interview since the midterms, we found him in a surprisingly reflective mood, and seemingly accepting of defeat.”

Trump was less than 24 hours away from proving that claim wrong, but “60 Minutes” still found zero minutes to press him on election denialism. Instead, it vouched for him.

I was disappointed but not surprised.

Under its new ownership and its editor-in-chief Bari Weiss, CBS News has a track record of going easy on Trump. An interview conducted by Douthat, with Weiss in tow, was never going to be combative or challenge Trump on election denialism — the core of his movement’s ideology.

So how did I see what the legacy media missed?

To start with, I listened to what Trump was saying. I read what he was posting. I took him literally and seriously.

Just as important, I had seen this pattern before. Less than a week after the GOP’s stinging defeat, Trump’s messaging was slowly but surely shifting from “I lost” to “Republicans lost” to “maybe Republicans didn’t lose at all.”

Donald Trump was never going to let an election loss pass without a lie. From the birther conspiracy about Barack Obama to the 2020 Big Lie and his ongoing efforts to relitigate that loss, election denialism has become the one requirement for membership in the MAGA movement.

Most importantly, I have no reason to look away.

This is the ethos I have infused in Democracy Docket. It has no corporate overlords and no other businesses that depend on access to the White House or favors from government officials. It doesn’t need to stay in Trump’s good graces.

That independence, and our commitment to democracy, allow Democracy Docket to tell the truth about Trump’s attacks on elections while other pundits and commentators stay silent.

And this is only the beginning. Trump’s post took aim at voting machines and early votes. It’s worth watching where that leads.

Officials may face pressure to delay or refuse certification. Early and mail voting may come under new attacks. There may be a push to change how votes are cast and counted before 2028.

Democracy Docket will be tracking and exposing every step.

That’s why Democracy Docket’s reach and influence keep growing. Most recently, it has added regular live podcasts to its free offerings to serve those in our community who prefer to hear from me on video.

For $10 a month or $120 a year, you’ll get my premium newsletters with analysis you won’t find anywhere else. You’ll also get members-only live events and access to our members-only community.

Most importantly, you’ll help keep Democracy Docket independent, so we can keep covering the stories the legacy media is ignoring.

The midterms may be over, but the fight to save democracy is only beginning. I’m proud to have you by my side.

items.title: The Democracy Election
items.author: 1axbxgygq0xjv9t9efsm9cfezkmplfrfffcijn@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
items.content:
When voters went to the polls Tuesday, democracy was on their minds.

Exit polls from the midterms show that 33% of voters named the state of democracy as the most important issue facing the country. By comparison, health care, foreign policy and crime all registered in the single digits. Only the economy ranked higher, at 39%.

For Democratic voters, the results were even starker. Nearly half (47%) ranked the state of democracy as their top issue. No other issue, including the economy, came close.

To paraphrase James Carville: for Democrats in 2026, it was democracy, stupid. As one prominent pollster put it to me, the new data is “consistent with our polls throughout the year, which showed that democracy was a top-tier motivator for Democrats.”

Conventional wisdom holds that democracy resonates mainly with older, college-educated voters, and some strategists dismiss the issue for that reason. That’s a mistake. These voters turn out at the highest rates, donate to campaigns and follow politics closely.

Most importantly, although these voters are now anti-Trump, they have not always been Democrats. In 2012, Mitt Romney won white college-educated voters, and the same group favored Republicans in the 2014 midterms.

Only since Trump’s arrival on the political scene has this group become a key part of the Democratic coalition. Some are so-called Never Trump Republicans; others are swing voters who have moved toward Democrats.

The bottom line: writing off democracy as an issue because it appeals to older, educated voters would be a serious error. Democrats do not have a lock on this cohort, and democracy is the issue that currently binds them most closely to a big-tent party with many other constituencies.

Then there are Black voters, who watched as the Supreme Court gutted what remained of the Voting Rights Act’s protections in . Republicans believed the decision would pave the way for replacing Black elected officials throughout the South. It had the opposite effect.

Black voters, the Democratic Party’s most reliable constituency, turned out in record numbers to prove that a conservative Supreme Court will not strip democracy and the right to vote from their community. If that isn’t pro-democracy action, nothing is.

Those who argue that economic issues weighed more heavily than democracy also need to explain why two of the most effective ad campaigns across the states focused on Trump’s refusal to fully release the Epstein files and the GOP’s support for data centers.

Neither fits neatly into an economic frame. Both, however, fit squarely within the set of issues that make up the pro-democracy cause.

The federal government’s failure to fully release the Epstein files was an easily understood example of an administration refusing to abide by the rule of law. The Justice Department’s complicity in withholding them angered those concerned with the separation of powers and constitutional limits on presidential power.

Opposition to data centers is likewise driven, at least in part, by a concern that wealthy Trump supporters are receiving preferential treatment while local communities are ignored. While some argue that this reflects a separate concern about corruption, I think that defines democracy too narrowly.

When people express concern about the state of democracy, they are not referring only to elections but to whether the consent of the governed still has meaning. Elections are central to democracy, but so are the rule of law and accountability for those who break it.

Trump’s attacks on our elections obviously made voters concerned about our democracy. But because he carried these attacks out by abusing the power of the federal government, the issue became broader than typical Republican voter suppression.

For the new majorities in Congress and Democratic state officials, taking the democracy issue seriously means more than paying lip service to the dozen or so pro-voting bills that are regularly discussed. They should think more boldly and expansively about how to protect democracy from the threats of the modern era.

Candidates considering a run for president or other office in 2028 must understand that democracy is the single most important issue for Democratic primary voters, and act accordingly. That means prioritizing it in their campaigns rather than treating it as a secondary concern.

The fate of democracy in the Trump era is the central issue of our generation. The 2026 midterms bore that out, and I expect 2028 will make it even more obvious.

The question is whether Democratic campaigns and officeholders will accept this or keep trying to explain it away in favor of traditional messaging.

For the sake of the party and the country, I hope they choose the former. It is our job to make sure they do.

items.content:
I have worked on campaigns for more than 30 years. I’ve represented presidential candidates who won and who lost, as well as candidates in Senate, House and gubernatorial races, in their moments of greatest joy, deepest despair and greatest uncertainty.

Elections are not won or lost in one night. They are the product of campaigns, cultural shifts, referendums on those in power and hopes for the future. But they are also the result of voting laws and rules.

If there is one lesson from 2026, it is that the rules of voting matter as much as anything else.

Donald Trump spent countless hours and taxpayer dollars trying to rig the rules to hold on to power. The Department of Justice systematically attacked our elections through lawsuits, intimidation and lies.

In the end, they failed, because lawyers litigated, election workers did their jobs and the American people voted.

Sadly, the legacy media largely ignored the real stakes of these long, hard-fought legal battles to protect voters and voting rights in the midterm elections.

Their coverage focused on the horse race and on who stood to benefit from each challenge. It ignored the question of right and wrong: Trump was trying to undo democracy, while those of us fighting back were working to protect it.

I am proud that Democracy Docket never shied away from these fights, and I am grateful that you were right there with us.

I started Democracy Docket in 2020 because the legacy media was failing to cover the onslaught of GOP attacks on free and fair elections. Today, more than 500,000 readers turn to us for news about what’s happening in the courts.

Throughout the midterm elections, from the gerrymandering battles to the post-election litigation, Democracy Docket’s team worked around the clock to bring you up-to-date news and analysis about efforts to subvert election results and disenfranchise voters.

No one followed the Justice Department’s lawsuits attacking our voting system more closely, and no other outlet provided the same depth of analysis.

In addition to my day job as a lawyer in these fights, I wrote essays and provided breaking news analysis on a near-daily basis through livestreams, during which I answered your questions.

That’s because Democracy Docket has never been a one-way platform. Speaking with you and hearing your feedback has always been a priority.

Our work is far from over. In many ways, the hardest part is still ahead. Ballots are still being tabulated, certification is ongoing and legal challenges remain.

Democracy Docket is on the ground in Mississippi, and we are watching and reporting on close elections around the country.

Though the work continues, we could not have gotten through this moment without you. Your messages inspire me, your optimism motivates me and your support keeps this work going.

Our members keep Democracy Docket’s website and podcasts free for everyone. Free content is core to our mission, which makes our Premium members essential. They powered us through the midterms, and they will power us through what comes next.

Premium members also receive my written analysis and invitations to members-only events. If you read my analysis while our paywall was down during the midterms, you already know what that includes.

If you’re not able to become a Premium member right now, I understand. As always, thank you for being a subscriber and reader. But if you do upgrade, I would deeply appreciate it.

Our work together is just beginning, and I’m honored to have you by my side during this new dawn for our democracy.

In 1946, a Black Army veteran was returning from World War II when a white police officer pulled him off a Greyhound bus and beat him blind.

The details were fuzzy. No one was sure about the identity of the police officer. The veteran, Isaac Woodard, didn’t even know what town he was in when it happened. Radio host Orson Welles learned about the shocking crime and pledged to find the officer who did it.

“We’ll call the policeman ‘Officer X,’” Welles said on his Sunday evening program. “He might be listening to this; I hope so. Officer X, I’m talking to you. Wash your hands. Scrub and scour, you won’t blot out the blood of a blinded war veteran.”

, the podcast brings us Woodard’s story, from his beating to the outrage that prompted the military’s desegregation. And to understand the experience of a Black servicemember today, we speak with Kyle Bibby, a Marine Corps veteran and co-founder of the Black Veterans Project.

items.title: What Harmeet Dhillon left out of her resignation letter
items.author: 1axckhtfz27exyoh2ko4cl96s1n5gdibde0yxv@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
items.content:
As the Department of Justice filed a flurry of lawsuits in the final weeks before the election to derail vote counting and certification, something was off. On my daily podcasts, I repeatedly asked: Where is Harmeet Dhillon?

Dhillon was the Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights and a former Republican election lawyer. She was the architect of DOJ’s failed lawsuits to gain access to state voter files. And yet, in the homestretch, she was missing from the biggest cases.

Finally, the mystery has been solved.

We now know that in early October, Dhillon told the White House she planned to leave after the election. Yesterday, she formally resigned.

Now the question is, what happened to one of Donald Trump’s staunchest promoters of disenfranchisement?

When Donald Trump prepared to take office for the second time, he made clear that he wanted the Department of Justice to serve his personal agenda. And nothing was more important to him than vindicating his discredited theory of election denialism.

This required transforming the Civil Rights Division into an attack dog that would limit voting rights rather than protect them. The person he chose to lead this effort was Dhillon.

When he nominated her in December 2024, he described her as “one of the top Election lawyers in the Country, fighting to ensure that all, and ONLY, legal votes are counted.” While Trump may have overstated her reputation slightly, there is no question that Dhillon lent an air of respectability to the election-denier cause.

A California lawyer with strong Republican Party credentials, she carried less baggage than those closely associated with Trump’s 2020 post-election debacle. For a while, Dhillon seemed perfectly positioned to succeed in the new MAGA administration.

Yet from the beginning, Dhillon ran into problems.

Her signature legal effort was obtaining complete voter data from every state. When 30 states and the District of Columbia refused, she sued them. These cases did not go well for her.

By Election Day, DOJ had lost 27 of those cases in district court and won none. It also lost the only appeals court ruling. The losses included more than a dozen defeats before Republican-appointed federal judges, nine of them appointed by Trump himself. DOJ was having scarcely more luck defending against lawsuits challenging the administration’s efforts to restrict voting by executive order.

Taken together, DOJ’s voting litigation resembled the same failed scheme Trump’s private lawyers launched after the 2020 election. As the defeats mounted, it seemed clear that something would have to change.

It seems that “something” was Dhillon.

Yesterday, Attorney General Todd Blanche announced that he had accepted her resignation. Dhillon’s letter to Trump, which lists her achievements, makes no mention of the voter roll lawsuits.

The only election-related accomplishment she cites is her deployment of election monitors. After much excitement, this too seemed to have fizzled in the end.

With Dhillon’s resignation made public, attention immediately turned to the reason for her exit.

Some suggested she might have jumped off a sinking ship of increasingly desperate, losing voting cases demanded by the White House. As I noted above, her name was conspicuously absent from the pleadings filed in California seeking to set aside 20,000 ballots, and in Alaska, where DOJ wanted to dictate certification.

The other possibility was that she was pushed out for leading a failed legal effort to achieve Trump’s election goals. Given her dismal record in court, this too seemed plausible.

Then, late in the day, CBS News reported a third possibility: that Trump demanded she be fired after watching her brief appearance on “60 Minutes” in mid-October, feeling she had not been forceful enough.

In most respects, the interview was standard fare. Dhillon toed the White House line on distrust in elections and noncitizen voting. While Trump may have wanted something more conspiratorial, she suggested that unspecified “irregularities” had marred past elections.

What I suspect landed her in trouble was this exchange:

What I’m hearing you say is that you think it’s very unlikely that a vote, a state vote, will be challenged. But people worry about that. Can you rule it out?

Well, I don’t know what is going to happen, but I can tell you that absent some shocking contingency that is unexpected, there should be no interruption in the usual course of counting and certifying the results in the states.

The problem for Dhillon is that by the time the interview aired, DOJ had already sued California to force an “interruption in the usual course of counting” ballots in that state. Indeed, DOJ was insisting that state and local officials ignore state law and set aside ballots from 20,000 people the administration had identified as potential noncitizens.

Meanwhile, DOJ was on the verge of filing an even more outrageous lawsuit that sought to block Alaska from certifying its Senate results if Trump’s preferred candidate lost.

In Trump’s orbit, it is impossible to know what really motivates hirings and firings. Dhillon, for her part, told Fox News she was not asked to resign. The truth may lie somewhere in between.

Dhillon may have been less effective than Trump wanted and more principled than he would tolerate. She may have had red lines she would not cross, in public or in private.

Either way, her legacy will be that of someone who came to DOJ to do Trump’s bidding and fell out of favor when she failed. In that, she joins a long list of others who have learned that with Trump, loyalty is a one-way street.

items.title: Why challenges to a fair count in Mississippi and Alaska will fall flat
items.author: delivery_20261105064035.48275920.3584@bounce.slate.com
items.content:
Tensions were high going into Election Day, not only because control of Congress was up for grabs but also because President Donald Trump and his administration had spent months attempting to interfere with states’ electoral processes. Lawsuits were filed, letters were sent, and threats were made, yet in the end Democratic candidates across the country notched definitive wins with margins that, in the words of Trump, were simply “too big to rig.” Even Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton—and Trump himself—was forced to concede defeat. The judiciary played a major role in tamping down frivolous legal challenges before the vote, and now Democrats, with their handsome majorities in both the House and Senate, have a mandate to fulfill. 

Consequentially, the two biggest legal challenges that consumed the days leading up to the midterms have effectively been shut down. The Department of Justice’s lawsuit against California election officials, which argued that they must set aside some 20,000 mail ballots the federal government suspected of being cast by noncitizens, was shut down by the U.S. Supreme Court on Monday. And the day before, a federal judge dismissed the DOJ’s lawsuit in Alaska, which sought to separate and preserve certain ballots cast in the state’s Senate election in the event that Republican Dan S. Sullivan lost his race. Across the country, in almost every instance of the DOJ suing states for access to their voter rolls, the federal government lost its case.

With all of that said, it’s worth looking at what the state of play is for any ongoing election challenges with a pair of major Senate races and a number of House seats yet to be called. The AFL-CIO, one of the largest national labor unions, sued the DOJ to stop it from demanding that state and local election officials separate disputed ballots and threatening prosecution if those ballots were counted. The case has been ping-ponging between judges at the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, and on Election Day, the AFL-CIO asked the full court to weigh in—all 29 federal judges—and it remains to be seen where that may take this case. Over in Alaska, there was also new DOJ activity; this time, the agency sent 20 Democrats letters informing them that they may be targets of a federal investigation over donor fraud and conspiracy charges and that they should preserve certain records. Among those who received the letters was Marc Elias, a well-known elections lawyer who has represented Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola, whose Alaska race has yet to be called. It’s not clear yet where this investigation will go, if anywhere, though Joyce Vance, a former U.S. attorney for the Northern District of Alabama, noted in her Substack: “The idea of prosecuting these people is odd since the Alaska Supreme Court has already determined that both Dan Sullivans could be on the ballot.”

These legal challenges, though significant, are not exactly to the tune of what was happening in the aftermath of the 2020 presidential election. In fact, the tone and temperature of the president and his allies have been markedly subdued since Tuesday night, with Vice President J.D. Vance putting out a surprisingly candid assessment of the Republican Party’s losses, while House Speaker Mike Johnson publicly acknowledged that the party had lost control of the House. Come Wednesday morning, Johnson also informed his staff that he does not intend to stay on as leader in the new Congress. To Charles Stewart III, a political scientist and professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, this more muted reaction is likely because there is a realization setting in that “these intellectual wars, election administration wars, are not getting them what they’re trying to achieve, either on the political side or on the strategic side.” 

Even if a worst-case scenario breaks out in which the Trump administration or Republican candidates challenge election results or processes in tight Senate races in Alaska or Mississippi, “the heavy hitters of both the Democratic and Republican parties, with respect to legal talent, will not be spread thin,” Stewart told me. “I think it will be much easier for attacks on the democratic process to be beaten back.” That is especially true when considering Democrats’ margins of victory in certain states, like Texas and Georgia, where their candidates earned double-digit wins. Even in races that were closer, Democratic candidates secured comfortable vote counts that largely fall outside margins of error. This gives way to a math problem that Republicans simply cannot solve for; Democrats have so far earned 54 seats in the Senate, a body that confirms election results, and the Trump administration does not have a meaningful enough majority of Republicans to pressure its legal shenanigans onto this time around.

“The margins last night are too big for DOJ meddling to make any sense, and it definitely won’t work,” Ankush Khardori, a former federal prosecutor, wrote. Harry Litman, a former U.S. attorney and deputy assistant attorney general, also expressed skepticism about meddling: “The most important defense/pushback/insurance policy against attempted election interference always has been a Democratic rout, which takes away the Trumpian bogus premise of a close election decided by illegal votes.” 

The bigger question now is if and how Democrats will use their congressional majorities. They will take over as chairs of the most powerful congressional committees capable of subpoenaing every single administration official, ally, or donor and deciding whether to penalize—or even possibly impeach—any of them for actions they’ve undertaken since Trump began his lawless second term.

items.title: Trump’s Alaska meltdown says it all
items.author: 1axbpx0vlef675kwd5p26396aqqssvrq070qub@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
items.content:
Judging by his social media post, Donald Trump agrees with me, which is why he is focused on Alaska as his last chance to keep the Democratic Senate sweep — and his humiliating defeat — from growing any larger.

Peltola holds a narrow lead, with more ballots still to be counted. What Trump continues to ignore is that those ballots will be counted and the results certified pursuant to state law. There is no legal path to reassigning votes.

In the run-up to the election, Trump directed his Department of Justice to accomplish in court what he is still demanding on social media today. DOJ lost — badly. It filed an appeal to the Ninth Circuit but has taken no steps to seek immediate review or relief.

The lawyers at DOJ no doubt understand what Trump does not: His effort to rig the Alaska Senate election failed. His assault on free and fair elections is over.

Indeed, Trump and his cronies are now likely to face a Congress eager to conduct oversight of their abuses of power, and that oversight is certain to include their attacks on democracy.

Nowhere will the administration face greater scrutiny than in the Democratic-controlled House of Representatives. While the Senate margins have garnered much of the attention, House Democrats romped from coast to coast.

Before the election, Democrats were expected to take control of the House, but with somewhere between 225 and 235 seats. Democrats have already been declared the winners in more than 250 races, and that number continues to climb.

No party has won more than 257 House seats in over three decades, a total Democrats reached in 2008. That came in a presidential election year, a historic one at that; meeting or exceeding that number in a midterm would be astounding.

All of these victories are even more impressive given the obstacles Donald Trump put in the way of voters, election officials and Democratic candidates.

He pressured big law firms to provide him with free legal services and intimidated them out of protecting voting rights. His Department of Justice launched more than 30 cases to undermine free and fair elections. He weaponized the criminal justice system against his political opponents.

Yet despite all of that, Trump and his party not only lost but were thoroughly repudiated.

There will be many theories about why Trump failed. Some will say it was the economy and affordability. Others will point to foreign wars or health care.

Yes, those issues — plus corruption and democracy — helped motivate voters and shaped their choice of candidates. But none of it would have mattered if the machinery of elections had failed.

As we celebrate the landslide repudiation of the GOP, we must remember how close we came to losing voters’ ability to elect the candidates of their choice.

In the days ahead, I believe we will celebrate Democrats gaining Senate seats in Mississippi and Alaska. I expect House Democrats to surpass 257 seats.

Once those results are certified and the celebrations have ended, it will be time for us to get to work. Never again should we have to fight the federal government to protect our elections. Never again should a president be empowered by his party to destroy democracy.

This is the defining fight of our generation. As soon as my legal work in the remaining elections is done, I am ready to take it on right here at Democracy Docket. I hope you will join me.

items.title: The Extraordinary Power of an Ordinary Act
items.author: bounce_ffd21a6f-9bd8-f111-bf5b-000d3a54442e_prod@bounce.myngp.com
items.content:
As an organization with the word “democracy” in its name, yesterday felt particularly special, unrelated to the actual results. It was special because the country did the ordinary extraordinary act of voting in massive numbers, responding with affirmation of the vision of the nation’s founders as “We the People.”   

After months of warnings about ICE at the polls and National Guard troops patrolling nearby, after threats of seized ballots and real efforts to challenge ballots in advance of a singe vote, after planning to protect the election officials who make this system work, and after worrying about and planning for all that could go wrong, Americans voted quietly and with dignity. They waited in line with patience, and their individual voices produced a loud response.

The political meaning of the results will be parsed for weeks and that is where we defer to the analysis of others. We, instead, see a nonpolitical message that is simple and crucial, no matter your political leanings. We see an electorate that said no to cruelty, no to hooded and disguised federal employees aggressively patrolling their streets and harming individuals, no to deplorable and inhumane detention conditions, and no to the deportation of their long-time friends, neighbors, classmates, and workers within their communities. We see an electorate that said it was tired of the grifting, the shouting, and the retribution.

Most importantly, we see an electorate that is begging for kindness and decency. We see an electorate that waited for its moment to say clearly that it wanted – no, needed – respect for themselves and for each other. 

To us, that is how to explain results that represent America far more than a political ideology. These new government leaders will include people from all walks of life – men and women from vastly different economic backgrounds, religions, ethnicities, family configurations, ages, and personal beliefs. 

There remains much work ahead. But today is a day to feel gratitude for an election that served as a fitting end-of-year tribute to the signing of the Declaration of Independence 250 years ago. The people met the vision and for that we should all be grateful.
